title: "Direct sampling & plots"

## Sample distribution
Every distribution in `m.dist` can be sampled **directly**, outside of a model, by passing
`sample=True`. This is useful for prior predictive checks, simulating data, or quickly inspecting a
distribution's shape.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
##### Python
```{python}
from BayesForge import bf
m = bf()
# Draw 1000 samples from a standard normal
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(4,), sample=True)
```

##### R
```r
library(BayesForge)
m <- importBF()
# Draw 1000 samples from a standard normal
m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(4L), sample=TRUE)
```

##### Julia
```julia
using PyBayesForge
using PythonCall
m = importBF()
# Draw 1000 samples from a standard normal
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape = (4,), sample=true)
```
:::

By using (`to_jax=False`), a direct sample is returned as a **`SampledData`** object — a thin wrapper
around a JAX array. It behaves like a JAX array everywhere (arithmetic, indexing, `jnp.*` functions,
`jit`/`vmap`/`grad`, use as a distribution parameter), and its `repr` reports the dtype so you can see
the kind and precision at a glance:


The extra thing a `SampledData` gives you over a raw array is a set of **built-in plotting methods** and **built-in helper functions**.

## Plotting helpers

Each plotting method is called directly on the sampled object. Most accept `interactive=True`
(the default, **Plotly**) or `interactive=False` (**matplotlib / seaborn**):


The available methods depend on the **shape** of the sampled array.

### 1D-(n_samples,)

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### histogram
::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
##### Python
```{python}
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,), sample=True, to_jax=False).hist() 
```

##### R
```r
m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(1000L), sample=TRUE, to_jax=FALSE)$hist()
```

##### Julia
```julia
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape = (1000,), sample=true, to_jax=false).hist()
```
:::

#### Time series — `(n_samples, n_time)`

Treat the second axis as time and summarise across draws.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
##### Python
```{python}
m.dist.gaussian_random_walk(scale=0.5, num_steps=50, shape=(500,), sample=True, to_jax=False).timeseries(credible_interval=0.9)
```

##### R
```r
m$dist$gaussian_random_walk(scale=0.5, num_steps = 50L, shape = reticulate::tuple(500L), sample=TRUE, to_jax=FALSE)$timeseries(credible_interval=0.9)
```

##### Julia
```julia
m.dist.gaussian_random_walk(scale=0.5, num_steps=50, shape = (500,), sample=true, to_jax=false).timeseries(credible_interval=0.9)
```
:::
:::

#### surface_3d

Computes a 2D Kernel Density Estimate (KDE) using the first two variables. It plots a 3D surface where the X and Y axes represent the variables and the Z axis represents the estimated probability density.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
##### Python
```{python}
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True, to_jax=False).surface_3d() 
```

##### R
```r
m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(1000L, 4L), sample=TRUE, to_jax=FALSE)$surface_3d()
```

##### Julia
```julia
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape = (1000, 4), sample=true, to_jax=false).surface_3d()
```
:::

#### scatter3d

Takes the first three variables (columns) and plots them directly as points in a 3D space (X, Y, and Z axes). Requires the array to have at least 3 variables (columns).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
##### Python
```{python}
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True, to_jax=False).scatter3d() 
```

##### R
```r
m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(1000L, 4L), sample=TRUE, to_jax=FALSE)$scatter3d()
```

##### Julia
```julia
m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape = (1000, 4), sample=true, to_jax=false).scatter3d()
```
:::

## Non-plot helper

In addition to plot helper functions, there are several other helper functions that can be used to compute summaries or transform the sampled array. For reduction operations (like `mean`, `std`, `sum`), you can pass an `axis` argument to reduce along specific dimensions. For example, passing `axis=0` will reduce across the sample dimension.

### mean
::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
##### Python
```{python}
m.dist.normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape=(100,4), sample = True, to_jax=False).mean(axis=0)
```

##### R
```r
m$dist$normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape = reticulate::tuple(100L, 4L), sample = TRUE, to_jax=FALSE)$mean(axis = 0L)
```

##### Julia
```julia
m.dist.normal(0,1, name = "a", shape = (100, 4), sample = true, to_jax=false).mean(axis=0)
```
:::

### .at[]

Since the sampled object wraps a JAX array, you can use JAX's `.at[]` syntax for in-place style updates (which return a new object):

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
##### Python
```{python}
s = m.dist.normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape=(100,4, 5), sample = True, to_jax=False)
s_new = s.at[0, 0, 0].set(0.0)
```

##### R
```r
s <- m$dist$normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape = reticulate::tuple(100L, 4L, 5L), sample = TRUE, to_jax=FALSE)
s_new <- s$at[0L, 0L, 0L]$set(0.0)
```

##### Julia
```julia
s = m.dist.normal(0,1, name = "a", shape = (100, 4, 5), sample = true, to_jax=false)
s_new = s.at[0, 0, 0].set(0.0)
```
:::

```{python}
m.dist.normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape=(100,4, 5), sample = True, to_jax=False).reshape((100, 20))
```

##### R
```r
m$dist$normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape = reticulate::tuple(100L, 4L, 5L), sample = TRUE, to_jax=FALSE)$reshape(reticulate::tuple(100L, 20L))
```

##### Julia
```julia
m.dist.normal(0,1, name = "a", shape = (100, 4, 5), sample = true, to_jax=false).reshape((100, 20))
```
:::

And many other standard NumPy/JAX array methods like `.flatten()`, `.squeeze()`, `.astype()`, etc., are also available directly on the sampled object.


## Notes

::: callout-note
- `density`, `surface_3d`, and `ppc_plot` are **Plotly-only** — passing `interactive=False` has no
  effect on them.
- The dimensional requirement is **enforced**: e.g. `corr_heatmap`, `boxplot`, `violinplot`,
  `pairplot`, `traceplot`, `scatter3d`, and `timeseries` raise a `ValueError` if the array is not the
  expected shape.
- Plotting methods live on the `SampledData` wrapper only. If you sampled with `to_jax=True` (or later
  called `.to_jax()`), convert back with `SampledData(arr)` to plot, or re-sample without `to_jax`.
:::
